rows.claim: Globalize (spec §5.1) MUST preserve: for a writer Y — allocate next index i, replace Y with `_w(p,i)`, create entry (Y,q) at index i in W_p, and spawn NO goal (globalizer is the receiver, expects value back); for a reader Y? — allocate next index i, replace Y? with `_r(p,i)`, spawn `global_send(Y?, _r(p,i), q)`, and create NO entry (globalizer keeps writer, sends value forward). The Gleam port must reproduce this exact direction verbatim.

Localize (spec §5.2) MUST preserve: for `_w(p,i)` — create fresh local pair (Y_q,Y_q?), replace with Y_q (writer), spawn `global_send(Y_q?, _w(p,i), p)`, create NO entry; for `_r(p,i)` — create fresh pair (Z_q,Z_q?), allocate next index k in W_q, add entry (Z_q,p,i), replace with Z_q? (reader), spawn NO goal. Gleam must reproduce this exact direction.

W_p lifecycle (spec §9.3, §13 Entry Lifecycle) MUST hold: an entry is created exactly once (by Globalize-writer OR Localize-reader, i.e. whenever the agent is the RECEIVER of a link) and removed exactly once (by Receive, when the assignment arrives and the writer is bound); an entry is NEVER modified between creation and removal. The serializer entry at index 0 is the only exception (updated, never removed).

Index allocation MUST use a SINGLE per-agent counter shared across both Globalize and Localize, starting at 1 (index 0 reserved for the serializer), with indices NEVER reused even after entry removal (Index Uniqueness invariant §13). Dart implements this as `int _nextIndex = 1` incremented by both addGlobalizeEntry and allocateIndex/addLocalizeEntry.

W_p create: Globalize-writer entry is created by addGlobalizeEntry(writerAddr, remoteAgent) which allocates the next index and stores GlobalizeEntry; Localize-reader entry is created by addLocalizeEntry(writerAddr, remoteAgent, remoteIndex) which throws ArgumentError on a duplicate (remoteAgent,remoteIndex) — enforcing the create-exactly-once invariant. Gleam port must preserve the duplicate-rejection guard.

W_p lookup MUST be two-kinded: GlobalizeEntries are looked up by DIRECT index (`_w(p,i)` case), LocalizeEntries by SEARCH over (remoteAgent, remoteIndex) (`_r(p,i)` case). Dart: lookupByIndex(index) returns _globalizeEntries[index]; findByRemote(agent,index) linear-scans _localizeEntries. The two entry kinds are stored in separate structures (Map<int,GlobalizeEntry> vs List<LocalizeEntry>).

W_p retire MUST be: removeGlobalizeEntry(index) deletes the index-keyed entry but is a NO-OP for index 0 (serializer permanent); removeLocalizeEntry(agent,index) removes the (agent,index)-matching entry. Both are idempotent (safe on non-existent). Gleam must keep index-0 retire as a guarded no-op.

The index-0 serializer entry MUST be initialized once at boot (mapping the local network-input writer N_p) and only ever UPDATED to a fresh writer, never removed. Dart: initializeSerializerEntry throws if re-initialized; updateSerializerWriter throws if not initialized; hasSerializerEntry/serializerWriterAddr expose state. Boot wires it via wp.initializeSerializerEntry(netInWriter).

The index-0 serializer is a many-to-one MERGE: multiple agents send to `_w(q,0)` simultaneously; the writer is reused in the message tail `[T|_w(q,0)]`; each received message extends q's network-input stream by one cell. The order of messages from DIFFERENT senders is non-deterministic, while messages from the SAME sender preserve FIFO order (Remark: Serializer as Merge). Gleam must reproduce merge semantics = stream extension + permanent entry update.

The merge-ordering guarantee the transport MUST supply: messages between any pair of agents are delivered in FIFO order (Message Ordering invariant §13) — if p sends two messages to q, q receives them in send order. This is the only ordering the correctness argument relies on; it is per-pair, not global. Gleam channel/transport must guarantee per-peer FIFO.

The `_send` kernel contract (`'_send'(T,G,Q)`, arity 3): INPUTS = T a term, G a struct `_w/2` or `_r/2` with a string agent arg and numeric index arg, Q an atom destination agent; PRECONDITION = runtime must be in madGLP mode (rt.madContext is a MadContext) else the kernel ABORTS; it delegates to ctx.send(termArg, isWriter, gnAgent, gnIndex, destAgent). Wrong arity / non-struct G / non-atom Q all abort. Gleam kernel must reproduce these argument checks.

FIDELITY RULE: `_send` MUST DEEP-dereference its term argument T before serialization — Dart uses _deepDeref (not _deref) because top-level-only deref leaves nested struct args as unresolved VarRefs, causing e.g. msg(bob,intro(alice,X)) to serialize as msg(VarRef,VarRef). A Gleam port that only shallow-resolves T will silently corrupt nested payloads.

What crosses the kernel boundary and its W_p/M_p side effects: ctx.send() extracts the term's variables, runs globalize() (which ADDS GlobalizeEntries to W_p for writers and returns global_send spawns for readers), registers the spawned global_send goals, substitutes global names into the term, then ADDS one OutboundMessage to M_p. So a single `_send` reduction mutates W_p (new writer entries) and M_p (one queued message) atomically.

`_send` payload format MUST branch on index: for a serializer address `_w(q,0)` the content is wrapped in a list cell `[T↑ | _w(q,0)]` (createSerializerPayload); for a normal `_w(p,i)`/`_r(p,i)` with i>0 the content is sent directly `G := T↑` (createGlobalSendPayload). Dart selects via `if (isWriter && gnIndex == 0)`. Gleam must reproduce the index-0 vs index>0 payload split.

`_send` ordering relative to the Reduce transaction: Reduce does NOT directly generate outgoing messages; instead binding a writer makes its reader X? known, which triggers a watching global_send goal, whose `'_send'` reduction adds the message to M_p. Send Atomicity invariant: the globalization of the term value (which may spawn further global_send goals) AND the addition of the message to M_p occur ATOMICALLY within the same Reduce transaction. Gleam must not split globalize and M_p-enqueue across transactions.

global_send predicate definition MUST be preserved verbatim: `global_send(T,G,Q) :- known(T) | '_send'(T,G,Q).` — guard known(T) succeeds only when T is bound to a non-variable term; `'_send'` globalizes T and adds message (G := T↑, Q) to the outgoing set M_p. The builtin is invoked ONLY when the guard succeeds (reader arg bound).

Reduce transaction (§8.1) MUST: on GLP reduction success (B,σ̂), apply σ̂ to bind writers and σ̂? to propagate to readers, move goals suspended on now-instantiated readers back to active, and set A'_p := (A_r·B·R)σ̂σ̂?. Case Suspend adds (A,W) to S_p when suspension set W≠∅; Case Fail adds A to F_p when W=∅. This is the unary agent-local reduction the Gleam engine already ports; the mad seam sits on top of it.

Send transaction (§8.2) MUST: when (m,q) ∈ M_p, remove it from M_p and place m in the communication channel to q, with destination q in the header and the assignment (global name + globalized term) in the body. Dart realizes Send as flushMessages() polling M_p per destination and invoking onMessageReady(dest,msg). All three transactions are unary (affect one agent).

Receive transaction (§8.3) MUST dispatch on three cases: `_w(p,i):=T` with i>0 → find entry (X,q) at index i, localize T from q, bind X, reactivate, REMOVE entry; `_w(q,0):=[T|_w(q,0)]` (serializer) → find permanent entry (N_q,*), localize T, assign N_q:=[T_q↓|N'_q], UPDATE entry to fresh writer (NOT removed); `_r(p,i):=T` → search entry (X_q,p,i) by (p,i), localize T from p, bind X_q, reactivate, REMOVE entry. Dart routes these in handleMadAssignment via isWriter/index==0.

global_send forwarding MUST be uniform: when an agent exports BOTH ends of a pair, the value flows Y_q → p's local pair (X,X?) → Z_q? via the SAME mechanism — no special forwarding logic in Receive. Receive simply binds the local writer and removes the entry; if that writer's reader X? is watched by a global_send goal (because it was also exported), that goal fires on a subsequent Reduce and forwards the value automatically. Gleam must NOT add ad-hoc forwarding; forwarding emerges from bind→global_send.
sources: docs/ma/madGLP-spec.md §4 Forwarding (lines 97), §8.3 Automatic Forwarding (lines 275), §5.4 worked example (lines 164-186)

rows.claim: On global_send, what LEAVES an agent (in order) is: (1) globalize the reader's now-known value T for destination Q — for each nested writer create entry (Y,Q) in W_p, for each nested reader spawn global_send(Y?,_r(p,k),Q); (2) exactly one message (G:=T↑, Q) enqueued to M_p; (3) later a Send moves it to the wire. For a cold-call the bytes are the list-wrapped `_w(Q,0):=[T↑|_w(Q,0)]`; for an established link the bytes are `G:=T↑` directly. Nested global names are baked with destination Q.

send_to_net/1 MUST be preserved as `send_to_net([msg(Q,T)|In]) :- global_send(T?, _w(Q,0), Q?), send_to_net(In?).` plus a `send_to_net([]).` base clause — cold-calls reuse the same 3-arg global_send with the well-known serializer address `_w(Q,0)` as G. Gleam Phase-A must keep cold-calls unified with established links (differ only in target address).

FIDELITY RISK (serializer tail encoding is an IMPLEMENTATION deviation the wire depends on): the spec says the serializer message reuses the actual writer `_w(q,0)` in the tail, but the Dart wire encodes the tail as a MARKER constant `ConstTerm('#serializer:agent:0')` and the receiver IGNORES the tail, allocating a fresh continuation writer itself. A Gleam port must byte-match this marker convention (or agree a new one on both ends) or serializer cold-calls will not decode.

FIDELITY RISK (writer/reader adjacency assumption): the Dart serializer encodes a writer's paired-reader id as `creatorLocalId + 1`, hard-assuming a writer cell and its paired reader occupy adjacent heap addresses. If the Gleam heap does not preserve the writer+1 = reader pairing convention, cross-agent assignment addressing (spec §5.3) silently breaks.

FIDELITY RISK (global_send fires on WRITER bind, not reader): despite the field being named readerAddr, GlobalSendSpawn.readerAddr is populated with the WRITER address and used as the heap.onBind key, because onBind is indexed by writer address and the goal must fire when the writer is bound (making the paired reader known). A Gleam port that literally watches the reader address will never fire global_send.

FIDELITY RISK (writer-globalize registers NO outgoing callback): per §5.1 a globalized writer creates entry (Y,q) and spawns nothing — agent p does NOT send anything for a `_w` entry, it only waits to RECEIVE. Dart explicitly omits onBind registration for globalize-writer entries. A Gleam port that installs a send-callback on globalized writers would double-send / invert direction.

FIDELITY RISK (v5.3 direction is easy to invert): the v5.3 spec explicitly CORRECTED the Globalize/Localize gs-vs-entry placement — writer→entry at the globalizer (receiver gets writer, sends value back); reader→global_send at the globalizer (globalizer keeps writer, sends value forward). Prior versions had it swapped. The Gleam port must follow v5.3, not any earlier mental model, or dataflow reverses.

BEYOND-SPEC (escalate for Phase-A scope): the Dart MadContext adds a duplicate-delivery dedup layer NOT in madGLP-spec.md — _deliveredWriterIndices / _deliveredReaderKeys, so a redelivered assignment whose W_p entry was already consumed is absorbed as a VERIFIED no-op (FR-021/SC-008) rather than throwing on the missing entry. Whether Phase-A Gleam must reproduce this reliability sublayer (vs. faithful-to-spec strict entry-required Receive) is a deviation decision to escalate, since faithful spec behavior would throw.

BEYOND-SPEC (escalate): the Dart Receive path routes all writer binding through a single bindAny seam (FR-035/SC-009) so an imported-reader target drains its suspensions while a local writer takes the plain bindVariable path. This local-pair-vs-imported-reader distinction is an implementation seam, not in the pure spec (which treats all variables as local pairs, §11.3). Gleam must decide whether to mirror bindAny or keep the spec's uniform-local-pair model.

The correctness yardstick the Gleam port is measured against is Theorem 5.7 ('the implementation (madGLP,π) of maGLP is correct'), where correct = live ∧ complete (Def. 2.3), resting on persistence/monotonicity (Lemma 5.2 / 3.12) and disjoint-substitution commutativity from SRSW (Lemma 3.20). There is deliberately NO confluence theorem (agent-level deterministic, system-level async non-deterministic). Preserve-exactly implications: unary Reduce→Send→Receive decomposition, per-pair FIFO, and write-once/read-once (SRSW).

Reserved system constants MUST be honored identically: `'_w(p,i)'` and `'_r(p,i)'` are global writer/reader names, `'_user'`/`'_net'` identify channels; underscore-prefixed constants are system-reserved and rejected in user mode (only `-mode(system).` files may use them). Gleam serialization uses functors `_w`/`_r` with (agent,index) args; the Dart deserializer recognizes exactly functor=='_w'/'_r' with 2 args. Gleam must keep the same functor spelling and reserved-name enforcement.

Initial configuration c0 MUST be: A_p = [agent(p, ch(_?,_), ch(_?,_))], S_p=F_p=M_p=∅, and W_p = {(N_p,*) at index 0} (serializer entry) — each agent boots with only its initial goal and the permanent index-0 serializer entry. Gleam boot must establish exactly the index-0 serializer entry before any goal runs; the Dart isolate/agent bootstrap does this immediately after enableMadGLP.

UI output is a DISTINCT local seam that MUST NOT be globalized: `send_to_ui([X|In]) :- ground(X?) | '_send_to_ui'(X?), send_to_ui(In?).` — the `ground(X?)` guard ensures no unbound variable crosses to Dart/Flutter, and `'_send_to_ui'` does NOT globalize, does NOT add to M_p, and creates no global links (purely isolate-local). This contrasts with network output (global_send, known(T) guard, globalization). Gleam must keep UI vs network output as two separate builtins with different guards.

Q5: The pure body-kernel outcome type is `KernelOutcome { KSuccess(heap, woken, output) | KAbort(detail) }` — two-valued: success carries the updated heap, reactivated GoalRefs, and captured output lines; abort carries only a String detail. It has NO channel for effectful state (W_p/M_p/index/messages).

Q5: The drive loop is three-tiered: scheduler.run loops scheduler.step (one reduction per dequeued goal), scheduler.step calls runner.reduce, and runner.reduce delegates to run_loop which recursively steps one bytecode instruction (Advance/Jump/Stop) until Proceed/Halt/suspend/fail.

Q5: The EXACT hook point for an effectful madGLP dispatch (_send etc.) is the BODY Spawn label-miss branch: when program.label_pc misses, the runner strips the /arity suffix and calls kernels.dispatch(ctx.heap, proc_name, arity, args). A _send builtin would be dispatched here.

Q5: kernels.dispatch is currently passed ONLY the heap (`dispatch(heap, name, arity, args)`) — it has no access to W_p/M_p/index/agent-state, so an effectful _send cannot be implemented there without changing the dispatch signature or routing effectful builtins on a parallel path.

Q5: The engine deliberately leaves `_now`/`_send` UNREGISTERED as kernels because they need wall-clock/IO the standalone engine lacks; a BODY Spawn to an unregistered kernel currently surfaces as a loud runner error (Malformed 'unresolved procedure/kernel'), never a guessed result.

Q5: kernels.is_kernel does NOT list `_send`; it enumerates only arithmetic/math/conversion/univ/mutual-ref/_output kernels, so is_kernel('_send',_) is False and a _send Spawn falls through to the unresolved-kernel error.

Q6: Heap immutability is total — every mutating heap op returns a NEW Heap value threaded through; bind_writer returns `Result(#(Heap, List(GoalRef)), HeapError)`, so bindings produce a fresh heap plus an activation list rather than mutating cells in place.

Q6: Dart's onBind callback is replaced by armed suspensions stored ON the WriterCell (heap.suspend_on_writer prepends a Suspension) plus heap.activate, which on bind_writer converts armed suspensions into GoalRefs; the cell is then replaced by a ValueCell so records never re-fire.

Q6: Woken-GoalRef reactivation is fully scheduler-driven: runner surfaces woken GoalRefs in ReduceOutcome.Reduced.woken, and scheduler.reactivate re-enqueues each woken goal (dedup per goal_id+generation) and clears it from the blocking table — this is the onBind replacement at the scheduler layer.

Q6: W_p/M_p/index can attach WITHOUT mutating the heap by threading them as additional immutable fields, exactly as the `output` line-capture channel already does: KSuccess.output → runner ctx.output → Reduced.output → Engine.output — a non-heap data channel already proven end-to-end.

Q6: A ready-made immutable model for the global-writers table W_p already exists: suspension.SuspensionTable is an opaque `Dict(Int, Set(Waiter))` with immutable suspend/consume/waiters_on operations (every op returns a new table) — the madGLP W_p (writer-id-keyed) can follow this exact shape.

Q6: Send/Receive transactions attach without in-place heap mutation because the scheduler Engine is itself an immutable opaque value — every scheduler.step returns a new Engine; madGLP transaction state can ride alongside the existing heap/queue/goals/blocking/next_id/output fields.

Q7: RECOMMEND a PARALLEL effectful path over widening KernelOutcome. Widening KernelOutcome would touch every kernel: all ~30 dispatch arms construct KSuccess(heap, woken, output) or bind_result/bind_term which return KSuccess with exactly three fields — adding a 4th (w_p/m_p/index) forces edits to every arm and every helper.

Q7: Widening also forces an engine-core change beyond kernels: runner's Spawn handler unpacks KSuccess(heap, woken, output) (runner.gleam:1874), ReduceOutcome.Reduced carries (heap, woken, spawned, output), and scheduler.step destructures Reduced(heap, woken, spawned, output) — a widened kernel outcome ripples through all three layers.

Q7: Proposed parallel effectful outcome type: `pub type MadOutcome { MadEffect(heap: Heap, woken: List(GoalRef), output: List(String), w_p: WritersTable, m_p: List(Message), index: Int, spawned: List(SpawnReq)) }` — the arithmetic/pure kernels keep returning KernelOutcome unchanged; only effectful builtins return MadOutcome, dispatched on a separate seam.

Q7: Proposed MadEngine wrapper over scheduler.Engine: `pub type MadEngine { MadEngine(engine: Engine, w_p: WritersTable, m_p: List(Message), index: Int) }` with `pub fn step(me: MadEngine, budget: Int) -> #(MadEngine, StepOutcome, List(Message))` and `run` = step looped — mirroring scheduler.run/step (run loops step, consuming one fuel per reduction).

Q7: The MadEngine wrapper CANNOT simply wrap scheduler.Engine as an opaque black box for _send, because the effectful state must be visible AT kernel-dispatch time inside runner.reduce (runner.gleam:1873), which is invoked deep inside scheduler.step — the opaque Engine boundary (scheduler.gleam:61) does not expose that inner call, so the effectful state has to be plumbed through runner.new_context / reduce.

Q7: runner.new_context builds a fresh RunnerContext from only (heap, regs); to give _send access to W_p/M_p/index the context (or reduce signature) must be extended — the RunnerContext currently has no field for agent-global effectful state (its non-heap channels are woken, spawn_reqs, output).

Q7: The scheduler already mints identity for body-spawned goals (spawn_goal assigns next_id and enqueues) and re-enqueues woken goals — so a madGLP Reduce transaction's spawned goals map cleanly onto the existing SpawnReq→spawn_goal path without new scheduler machinery.

Q8: term_codec ALREADY provides the global-name wire form: GlobalVarId(agent_id: String, local_id: Int) with tag 0x07 varref and encode_global_var_id/decode_global_var_id — an agent-scoped (p, i) identity that A0-A1 _w(p,i)/_r(p,i) global names and message serialization can REUSE directly.

Q8: term_codec's encode_term/decode_term handle a VarRef carrying a GlobalVarId (tag 0x07) across processes — the cross-process message body codec that Send/Receive need for terms is already present and byte-parity-tested; a `message` payload can be built from encode_term over its argument terms.

Q8: The parser ALREADY produces the two madGLP goal shapes: SpawnGoal(InnerGoal, agent_id) from `Goal@AgentId` and RemoteGoal(target, inner) from `Var#Goal` / `Module#Goal` — so remote-send surface syntax is parsed today; A0-A1 must reuse these AST nodes rather than add new syntax.

Q8: The parser produces `=..` (univ) goals (`Var =.. Expr`, `foo(a,b) =.. L`) as ast.Goal('=..', ...) — globalize/localize that decompose/compose a compound into functor+args can reuse this univ surface plus the existing runtime univ kernels _list_to_tuple/_tuple_to_list (kernels.gleam:88-89).

Q8 GAP (propose-first, Language Authority): there is NO `_w(p,i)`/`_r(p,i)` global-name literal syntax in the parser and no `message`/`globalize`/`localize` construct; terms.Term has only ConstTerm/StructTerm/VarRef(addr: Int), where VarRef is a LOCAL heap address with no global identity. Representing a global name in the engine's Term model needs either a sentinel StructTerm (as `$mutual_ref` does) or a NEW Term variant — the latter is a language extension requiring Gabi's approval.

Q8: A sentinel-struct precedent for a runtime-only special term exists: kernels represents the mutual-reference cell as `StructTerm("$mutual_ref", [ConstInt(addr)])` because Gleam's Term has no custom cell — a global-name `_w(p,i)` could analogously be `StructTerm("_w",[p,i])` WITHOUT a language-level Term change, keeping A0 inside existing authority.

COMPLETENESS RISK: The effectful outcome CANNOT currently carry messages up to the scheduler. StepReduced only reports (goal_id, procedure, woken, spawned) — there is no outbound-message field, so M_p emissions from a reduction have no path to surface at the scheduler step boundary without widening StepOutcome or a parallel step return.

COMPLETENESS RISK: The only non-heap data that reductions currently propagate to the Engine is `output` (captured print lines), threaded via list.append(engine.output, out) in scheduler.step; there is no analogous accumulator for outgoing messages M_p or for a global index counter, so both are ABSENT engine capabilities the madGLP port must add.

COMPLETENESS RISK: A KAbort from a body kernel is currently treated as a fatal RunnerError (Malformed, stops the reduction) — if _send's failure modes (e.g. transport error) are non-fatal in madGLP, the existing KAbort→RunnerError mapping at the Spawn site is too strict and needs a distinct effectful-failure outcome, not a reuse of KAbort.

Q6/Q7: The generation-scoped WakeKey/RunQueue dedup (enqueue_wake keyed by goal_id+generation) means a Receive that binds a writer will reactivate waiting goals at-most-once per generation — madGLP Receive can rely on the existing FR-005 reactivation machinery rather than inventing its own wake protocol.

Q6: Binding a global writer to satisfy a Receive uses heap.bind_writer, which returns the woken GoalRefs to re-schedule — so localize/Receive delivering a value into a local writer integrates with reactivation for free, provided the global name maps to a local heap writer address at delivery time.

The current link seam models a link END as a record-of-functions vtable Endpoint(id, send, recv, close, faults), NOT a stdio triple; send is fn(BitArray)->Result(Nil,LinkFaultSignal), recv is fn()->Result(Option(BitArray),LinkFaultSignal), close is fn()->Nil, and faults is a gleam_erlang process.Subject(LinkFaultSignal). This is the natural attach point for a (role,channel-identity) registry: each logical channel is one Endpoint value.

The seam is deliberately BILATERAL: 'the seam exposes exactly two logical ends; a broker is a transport relay UNDER one endpoint pair, never a logical hub' (FR-005). A (role,channel) registry that fans one physical carrier out to N logical channels must therefore live ABOVE the endpoint pair, not by turning an endpoint into a hub.

LinkId is a stable, never-reused identity LinkId(scheme:LinkScheme, endpoint:LinkAddress, nonce:LinkNonce) whose record value-equality is the idempotency-at-identity basis (FR-007): re-setup with the same LinkId returns the already-established link. It is a per-CONNECTION identity, not a per-logical-channel-role tag.

LinkNonce keeps NonceInt and NonceStr distinct on purpose ('an integer 5 is NOT the string 5') so equality matches the GLP term exactly; a channel-tag namespace layered on top must preserve this int/string distinction or it will alias two distinct logical channels.

RESOLUTION Q10(a): channel identity should be a SEPARATE lightweight role+index/channel-tag namespace ABOVE the transports, not a reuse of LinkId. LinkId already encodes scheme+endpoint+nonce for one physical bilateral link (link_id.gleam:24-26); the link-primitives contract explicitly defers full logical channel/writer-reader distribution ('glink') to a LATER higher-level layer built ON the base, dependency direction base->glink never the reverse.

RESOLUTION Q10(b): the stderr-equivalent is the FAULT/MONITOR stream, not a distinct diagnostic data channel. link_monitor/2 returns a per-link Faults monitor stream that is 'Independently observable from the data path (FR-008): reading Faults does not touch In/Out, and vice versa' — the third distinguished channel role IS the monitor stream, carried as ordinary bound ground terms (ok/tempFail/permFail/closed), never a 4th unification verdict (FR-043).

The seam already carries a fault channel out-of-band on Endpoint.faults:Subject and a coarse LinkFaultKind lattice {Closed,Transient,Permanent}; the GLP reliability sublayer refines these into ok/tempFail/permFail/closed ground terms. This confirms the diagnostic/stderr role maps onto the existing fault/monitor stream shape, distinct from send/recv data.

RESOLUTION Q10(c): logical channel identity being first-class is satisfied by EITHER physical-multiplexing choice because the seam is term-agnostic — it 'carries the byte-parity payload blob as an opaque frame and knows nothing about terms'. Distinct-carriers = one Endpoint per (role,channel); tagged-on-one-carrier = one Endpoint whose opaque frames carry a channel-tag prefix demuxed above the seam. Neither leaks into the transport leaf, so parity is preserved either way.

The tagged-on-one-carrier option is directly supported by the frame contract: send delivers 'exactly one self-delimiting frame' in submission order (FR-018) and recv returns one complete frame; a channel-tag can ride inside the opaque payload with no transport change, since FrameCodec/038-TLV sits ABOVE the endpoint (T046) and the endpoint is byte-agnostic.
Q11 dependency set: Phase-A runtime deps are exactly gleam_stdlib (>=0.34,<2.0) and gleam_erlang (>=0.34,<2.0); dev-dep gleeunit. No other runtime deps.

Q11 no-OTP policy CONFIRMED: 'The Gleam OTP actor package is intentionally NOT a dependency: its proc_lib use is outside AtomVM's BEAM/OTP subset, so the downstream port stays AtomVM-runnable by spawning the raw erlang way + gleam_erlang Subjects' — verified transitively absent per manifest.toml.

Q11 Phase-B primitives already demonstrated within the no-OTP subset: the loopback transport builds channel processes and a hub process using only gleam_erlang process.spawn / process.new_subject / process.receive(_forever) / process.send — the exact spawn-the-raw-erlang-way + Subject mailbox primitives Phase-B process-per-agent needs, WITHOUT gleam_otp.

Q11 RISK: a Phase-B process-per-agent design that reaches for gleam_otp supervisors/actors/gen_server for lifecycle would VIOLATE the ratified no-OTP policy (proc_lib outside AtomVM subset); Phase B must stay on raw process.spawn + Subject (as loopback already does) to keep AtomVM-runnable.

Q12 mapping: global_send/send_to_net/send_to_ui are ground-relay outbound roles; each maps to a distinguished logical channel whose payload is appended (ground-gated) to that channel's Out stream. In the seam this is Endpoint.send(BitArray) on the Endpoint bound to that (role,channel); send_to_ui specifically corresponds to the ground-only transport discipline the base layer adopts ('_send_to_ui guards ground/1, never globalizes').

Q12 ordering parity: byte/ordering parity vs the Dart oracle is asserted by (a) 038 TLV term codec being byte-for-byte identical against golden vectors corpus.hex, and (b) FrameCodec envelope parity (header/flags/sequence/CRC32 identical to Dart/C#) so any two runtimes interop. The channel demux must not perturb these bytes.

Q12 per-link FIFO parity is guaranteed at the transport level: loopback exchanges frames over two ordered in-memory channels 'FIFO / in-order / exactly-once by construction (FR-018/020)', and its channel_loop hands a parked reader the frame straight over preserving submission order.

Q12 TCP wire parity: each opaque frame is prefixed by a 4-byte BIG-ENDIAN length (<<len:int-size(32)-big, frame:bits>>) 'byte-identical to Dart/C#', so one send => one peer recv; a multiplexed channel-tag must sit INSIDE this length-prefixed opaque frame to keep the framing byte-identical to the Dart oracle.

Q12 cross-runtime assertion mechanism: parity is gated by 16 runs = 8 scenarios (pc_integers,pc_strings,pc_terms,link_send_wrapper,link_recv_chain,bidirectional,path_b_request_accept,monitor_close) x 2 directions, C#<->Gleam, all passing, across TCP (full 16/16), loopback (same-host pairs), QUIC-WS (WSL); a quiescence oracle (GAP-G6) decides completion before verdict comparison.

RISK (madGLP fidelity): the seam has NO cross-channel ordering guarantee — LinkOptions notes backpressure_window default 8 gives 'no head-of-line blocking ACROSS independent links', i.e. independent channels/links are intentionally unordered relative to each other. A Phase-B process-per-agent that races an index-0 serializer merge order across per-agent mailboxes could reorder relative to the single-process oracle, breaking parity, because the seam only promises PER-link FIFO, not cross-channel order.

RISK (physical-multiplexing leaking into logical identity): loopback derives LinkId nonce from a hub counter (NonceInt(n)) and TCP derives nonce from the PORT (NonceInt(port)) — physical/carrier facts. If a (role,channel) registry keys off LinkId, the logical channel identity would inherit carrier-specific nonces (port, hub counter), coupling logical identity to the physical multiplexing choice — the exact leak the DECIDED design forbids. A separate channel-tag namespace avoids this.

RISK (loopback self-rendezvous): a single OS process 'cannot rendezvous with itself' on loopback — the first arrival BLOCKS in process.receive until the peer appears. A Phase-B process-per-agent topology on one BEAM node must pair distinct spawned processes for each channel or a channel setup deadlocks; hermetic tests explicitly spawn one side.

RISK (fault-not-fail invariant must survive multiplexing): a fault NEVER becomes a unification verdict (FR-043) and a disconnect NEVER maps to a logical Fail (FR-044). If distinct logical channels are multiplexed onto ONE carrier, a single carrier fault would signal ALL multiplexed logical channels at once — the registry must fan the one LinkFaultSignal to every affected (role,channel) as data, without turning any into a logical failure.

RISK (recv is single-reader per Endpoint): the loopback channel_loop parks exactly ONE pending reader ('the single reader'); tagged-on-one-carrier multiplexing therefore cannot have N logical channels each independently blocking on the same physical Endpoint.recv — a demux pump must own the single recv and route frames to per-channel mailboxes.

RISK (scheme registry vs channel registry conflation): LinkScheme keys the TRANSPORT registry (T050) by scheme token (loopback|tcp|quic), a different namespace from a (role,channel) identity registry. Reusing the scheme-keyed selection path for channel identity would collide transport selection with logical channel demux — the channel registry is a distinct layer.

RISK (idempotency-at-identity vs channel setup): re-setup with the same LinkId returns the already-established link (FR-007). If two logical channels of the same role accidentally share a LinkId (e.g. both derive the same nonce), the second setup silently REUSES the first channel instead of creating a distinct one — the channel-tag namespace must guarantee uniqueness independent of LinkId nonce derivation.

The seam commits to synchronous Result + gleam_erlang Subject as a LANGUAGE-MAPPING choice (not a GLP-semantic deviation) because it is a HOST interface BELOW GLP; the frozen 025 semantics live ABOVE the seam in the primitives (T050). A (role,channel) registry therefore belongs in the primitives layer above, keeping the transport seam channel-agnostic.

RISK (TCP one-link-per-listen MVP): the TCP leaf accepts exactly one client then closes the listener ('One link per listen (MVP): release the port for re-use'). Distinct-carriers multiplexing of many logical channels over TCP would need many ports/listens; this MVP constraint limits how many distinct physical carriers a single (role) can hold concurrently.
